title: Unveiling the antiviral inhibitory activity of ebselen and ebsulfur derivatives on SARS-CoV-2 using machine learning-based QSAR, LB-PaCS-MD, and experimental assay

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract vs. Results section (MLR and ANN model statistics)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Abstract reports training set R² values of 0.83, 0.82, and 0.92 for MLR, RF, and ANN models respectively, and test RMSE values of 0.27, 0.18, and 0.09. However, the Results section reports substantially different values: MLR training R² = 0.69 (not 0.83), MLR test RMSE = 0.56 (not 0.27), ANN training R² = 0.89 (not 0.92), and ANN test RMSE = 0.05 (not 0.09). Only the RF values are consistent across both sections (R² = 0.82, test RMSE = 0.18). The discrepancy in MLR metrics is particularly large: the Abstract overstates MLR training R² by 0.14 and understates its test RMSE by more than a factor of 2 (0.27 vs 0.56). The Discussion/Conclusion section correctly references the Results values (ANN R² = 0.89, test RMSE = 0.05), confirming that the Abstract, not the Results, contains the erroneous values. This is a material error because the abstract is the most-read section of the paper and these numbers directly affect the perceived quality of the models.

The paper states 'pIC₅₀ = (1 / IC₅₀ (M))' as Equation 1 for converting IC₅₀ values to pIC₅₀. The standard and universally accepted definition of pIC₅₀ in pharmaceutical and QSAR literature is pIC₅₀ = -log₁₀(IC₅₀), where IC₅₀ is expressed in molar (M) units. The formula shown (1/IC₅₀) would produce numerically different values and is not equivalent to the negative logarithm transformation. For example, an IC₅₀ of 1 μM (10⁻⁶ M) would give pIC₅₀ = 6 by the standard formula, but 10⁶ by the formula shown. This could be a rendering or transcription artifact in the markdown version (the original PDF may display the correct logarithmic formula), which is why confidence is moderate rather than high. If the paper actually used 1/IC₅₀ rather than -log₁₀(IC₅₀) for the QSAR modeling, this would constitute a serious methodological error.

The text states: 'Gini importance varies between 0 and 1, with 0 representing the lowest and best possible importance. A higher Gini importance indicates greater.' This sentence is internally contradictory: if 0 represents the 'lowest' importance, it cannot simultaneously be the 'best' possible importance. The second sentence correctly states that higher Gini importance indicates greater importance, confirming that 0 is the lowest (worst, not best) importance. This appears to be a writing error where 'best' was used instead of 'worst', rather than a substantive scientific error. The contradiction does not affect the paper's conclusions, as the actual feature selection was performed correctly using the standard interpretation that higher Gini = more important.

summary: Verification of this published Scientific Reports paper (2025, 15:6956) on QSAR/machine learning for SARS-CoV-2 ebselen/ebsulfur inhibitors identified one high-confidence error and two lower-confidence issues. The high-confidence finding (confidence 0.90) is a data inconsistency between the Abstract and the Results section: the Abstract reports R² and RMSE values for MLR and ANN models that differ substantially from the actual values reported in the detailed Results section. Specifically, the Abstract overstates MLR performance (R²=0.83 vs actual 0.69) and understates its error (test RMSE=0.27 vs actual 0.56), while also misreporting ANN statistics (R²=0.92 vs actual 0.89; RMSE=0.09 vs actual 0.05). The Discussion section correctly references the Results values, confirming the Abstract is the erroneous section. This warrants a formal correction (erratum) to the abstract. Two additional lower-confidence issues were noted: (1) Equation 1 shows pIC₅₀ = 1/IC₅₀ instead of the standard pIC₅₀ = -log₁₀(IC₅₀), though this may be a markdown rendering artifact; and (2) a self-contradictory description of Gini importance ('0 representing the lowest and best possible importance'). Citation verification across 9 key reference claims found no fabricated citations or attribution mismatches. The paper's core scientific contributions (QSAR models, enzyme assays, LB-PaCS-MD simulations) appear methodologically sound based on text verification; the errors are primarily in the reporting of statistical metrics in the abstract.
